title: 08 — Data Contracts and Quality Gates
html:
08 — Data Contracts and Quality Gates

The one idea: a data contract is a versioned, machine-readable promise about a dataset — its schema, meaning, quality rules and freshness. The quality gate is the code that enforces that promise at the boundary between layers: data that keeps the promise is published atomically, data that breaks it is quarantined with a reason.

1. Definitions

  • Data contract: an agreement between a data producer and its consumers, written as a file (YAML) kept in git, covering schema, semantics, quality expectations, service levels, ownership and terms of use.
  • ODCS (Open Data Contract Standard): an open, vendor-neutral YAML standard for such contracts, maintained under the Linux Foundation (Bitol project). Version 3 is current.
  • Quality gate: an automated checkpoint (Bronze → Silver, Silver → Gold) that evaluates the contract against a batch and decides pass, warn or fail.
  • Quarantine: where failed records (or whole batches) go, with the failing rule, so a person can fix and re-release them.

2. Anatomy of an ODCS v3 contract

apiVersion: v3.0.2                  # ODCS version the file follows
kind: DataContract
id: silver-nav-daily
name: Daily mutual fund NAV
version: 1.3.0                      # contract version — semver
status: active
domain: funds
description:
  purpose: One validated NAV per plan per business day.
  limitations: NAV for a holiday is not published and must not be interpolated.

schema:
  - name: nav
    physicalName: silver.nav
    physicalType: table
    properties:
      - name: isin
        logicalType: string
        physicalType: string
        required: true
        primaryKey: true
        primaryKeyPosition: 1
        description: ISIN of the plan/option
        logicalTypeOptions: { pattern: "^IN[EF][A-Z0-9]{8}[0-9]$" }
      - name: nav_date
        logicalType: date
        required: true
        primaryKey: true
        primaryKeyPosition: 2
      - name: nav
        logicalType: number
        physicalType: decimal(18,4)
        required: true
        quality:
          - type: library
            rule: rangeCheck            # illustrative; see the standard for the exact quality-rule vocabulary
            mustBeGreaterThan: 0
    quality:
      - type: sql
        description: Day-on-day NAV move above 20% is suspicious
        query: |
          SELECT count(*) FROM (
            SELECT nav / lag(nav) OVER (PARTITION BY isin ORDER BY nav_date) - 1 AS move FROM ${object}
          ) WHERE abs(move) > 0.20
        mustBeLessThan: 1
      - type: sql
        description: No duplicate keys
        query: SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT (isin, nav_date)) FROM ${object}
        mustBe: 0

slaProperties:
  - property: freshness
    value: 1
    unit: d
    element: nav.nav_date
  - property: latency
    value: 4
    unit: h

team:
  - username: funds-data-owner
    role: owner
support:
  - channel: "#funds-data"
    url: https://chat.example/funds-data

Field names above follow the shape of ODCS v3; always check the current standard for the exact property names, especially in quality and slaProperties.

2.1 What goes in a contract — checklist

Section Questions it answers
Fundamentals What is it, who owns it, which version, which status
Schema Columns, types, keys, nullability, allowed patterns, units
Semantics What each field means, what it does not mean
Quality Rules that must hold, with thresholds
SLA Freshness, latency, availability, retention
Terms Allowed uses, licence restrictions, personal data classification
Support Who to contact, how to report a breach

3. Contract tooling: datacontract-cli

pip install "datacontract-cli[duckdb]"

datacontract lint  datacontract.yaml           # is the contract itself valid?
datacontract test  datacontract.yaml           # run schema + quality checks against the configured server
datacontract export --format sql datacontract.yaml          # generate DDL
datacontract export --format jsonschema datacontract.yaml   # generate a JSON Schema
datacontract changelog v1.yaml v2.yaml         # what changed between versions

Put lint and a breaking-change check in CI: a pull request that removes a required column or narrows a type must bump the major version and notify consumers.

Change Version bump
Add optional column, add a rule that current data passes Minor
Fix a description Patch
Remove/rename column, tighten type, make field required Major — breaking

4. The quality gate — what to check

Order checks from cheap to expensive, and from "file is unusable" to "number is suspicious":

# Category Examples Typical action
1 Structural File parses, expected columns present, encoding Fail whole batch
2 Schema & type Types cast, required fields present, patterns (ISIN regex + check digit) Fail row
3 Domain & range NAV > 0, rating in allowed scale, dates not in future Fail row
4 Uniqueness & referential No duplicate keys; every ISIN exists in the instrument master Fail row
5 Internal consistency Assets = liabilities + equity; segment totals = reported total Fail or warn
6 Statistical drift Row count within ±3σ of trailing mean; NAV move > 20%; null rate jump Warn, hold for review
7 Cross-source Two sources disagree on the same fact beyond tolerance Route to triangulation (chapter 10)
8 Freshness Latest nav_date older than SLA Alert owner

4.1 Rules as data

Keep thresholds and rules in a versioned table (or in the contract), not hard-coded:

CREATE TABLE quality_rule (
  rule_id        text PRIMARY KEY,
  dataset        text NOT NULL,
  severity       text CHECK (severity IN ('fail', 'warn')),
  sql_check      text NOT NULL,        -- returns failing rows
  threshold      numeric,
  effective_from date NOT NULL,
  effective_to   date NOT NULL DEFAULT '9999-12-31',
  approved_by    text NOT NULL
);

Now "why did this batch pass in June but fail in July?" has an answer: the rule changed on 1 July, approved by a named person.

4.2 A gate implementation with DuckDB and Polars

import duckdb, polars as pl
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class RuleResult:
    rule_id: str
    severity: str
    failed_rows: pl.DataFrame

def run_gate(batch: pl.DataFrame, rules: list[dict]) -> tuple[pl.DataFrame, list[RuleResult]]:
    con = duckdb.connect()
    con.register("batch", batch)
    results = []
    for r in rules:
        failed = con.sql(r["sql_check"]).pl()           # each rule returns the row_ids it rejects
        results.append(RuleResult(r["rule_id"], r["severity"], failed))

    hard_fail_ids = pl.concat([x.failed_rows.select("row_id") for x in results if x.severity == "fail"]
                              or [pl.DataFrame({"row_id": []}, schema={"row_id": pl.Int64})])
    passed = batch.join(hard_fail_ids, on="row_id", how="anti")
    return passed, results

rules = [
    {"rule_id": "nav_positive", "severity": "fail",
     "sql_check": "SELECT row_id FROM batch WHERE nav <= 0"},
    {"rule_id": "isin_known", "severity": "fail",
     "sql_check": "SELECT b.row_id FROM batch b ANTI JOIN read_parquet('ref/instruments.parquet') i USING (isin)"},
    {"rule_id": "big_move", "severity": "warn",
     "sql_check": """SELECT row_id FROM (
                        SELECT row_id, nav / lag(nav) OVER (PARTITION BY isin ORDER BY nav_date) - 1 AS m
                        FROM batch) WHERE abs(m) > 0.2"""},
]

4.3 Quarantine table

CREATE TABLE quarantine (
  quarantine_id  bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  dataset        text NOT NULL,
  manifest_id    text NOT NULL,       -- which landed file
  row_ref        jsonb NOT NULL,      -- the record or its key
  rule_id        text NOT NULL,
  detail         text,
  status         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open'   -- open | fixed | accepted | rejected
                 CHECK (status IN ('open','fixed','accepted','rejected')),
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  resolved_by    text,
  resolved_at    timestamptz
);

4.4 Atomic publish

Passing rows are written to Silver in one Iceberg commit (with table.transaction() in PyIceberg, or write-audit-publish on a branch). Consumers either see the whole batch or none of it; a half-published day never exists.

---
title: Quality gate between Bronze and Silver
---
flowchart LR
    B["Bronze batch<br/>(one manifest)"] --> S1["Structural checks"]
    S1 -->|fail| QB["Quarantine whole batch"]
    S1 --> S2["Row checks:<br/>schema, range, keys"]
    S2 -->|failed rows| QR["Quarantine rows"]
    S2 --> S3["Batch checks:<br/>drift, consistency"]
    S3 -->|warn| HOLD["Hold for review"]
    S3 -->|pass| PUB["One atomic commit to Silver"]
    PUB --> CARD["Quality card<br/>(scores per rule)"]

4.5 Quality cards

For each published batch, store a small summary — rows in, rows passed, rules evaluated, warnings, score — linked to the Iceberg snapshot ID. A consumer can then ask "how good was the data I used?" and get a precise answer.

5. Observability: freshness, volume, schema, distribution

The quality gate checks each batch. Monitoring watches trends across batches:

  • Freshness: time since the last successful commit per table.
  • Volume: rows per batch versus history.
  • Schema: unexpected new or missing columns at Bronze.
  • Distribution: null rate, distinct count, mean/percentiles per key column.

More in Orchestration, quality and governance.

6. Questions to test yourself

  1. Which contract changes are breaking, and how should CI react to them?
  2. Why store quality rules with effective dates and approvers?
  3. Design a drift rule for daily row count that does not fire on public holidays.
  4. What is the difference between failing a row and failing a batch? Give one rule of each kind.
  5. How do you guarantee consumers never see half a batch?

7. Review checklist

  • Every Silver and Gold table has a contract in git with an owner.
  • datacontract lint and a breaking-change check run in CI.
  • Rules are data, versioned, with approvers.
  • Failed rows land in quarantine with the rule ID and source manifest.
  • Publishing is one atomic commit; a quality card is stored per snapshot.
